text: Jan Kalicki (28 January 1922 – 25 November 1953) was a Polish mathematician known for his work on logical matrices. He graduated from high school in Warsaw in May 1939, just months before Germany invaded Poland on 1 September. He intended to attend the University of Warsaw but it was closed on 27 September when Poland surrendered. In response, prominent mathematicians such as Borsuk, Łukasiewicz, Mazurkiewicz, Sierpiński, Mostowski, and Kuratowski established an underground University of Warsaw to continue academic work, which was later repressed by the Nazis who imprisoned or killed several participants. Kalicki completed his studies in mathematics and philosophy at this underground institution, though he was not awarded his MA in mathematics and philosophy until after the war ended in 1945. After the war, he taught for two years at the Universities of Łódź and the University of Warsaw. He then went to London on a British Council Scholarship for two years, where he married Mireya Jaimes-Freyre in 1947 and had a son named after his father. In July 1948, he received his doctorate in mathematical logic from the University of London. Feeling that returning to Poland would be restrictive, he decided to stay in London and lectured in mathematics at Woolwich Polytechnic. The following year, he moved to the University of Leeds, where he remained until 1951. That year, he went to the United States to become a Visiting Assistant Professor of Mathematics at the University of California, Berkeley. In 1953, shortly after arriving, he was appointed Assistant Professor of Mathematics at the Davis campus and later returned to Berkeley to become Assistant Professor of Philosophy. He died three months later in a car accident north of Berkeley, California. A tribute from the University of California noted that he was beloved by colleagues and students. During the five years before his death, Kalicki published 13 papers on logical matrices and equational logic.
